hero-couple: “Now that we’re living in Objectville, we’ve just got to get into Design Patterns… everyone is doing them.”
“Soon we’ll be the hit of Jim and Betty’s Wednesday night patterns group!”
duck-subclasses: Duck: quack(), swim(), display(), // other duck-like methods…
MallardDuck: display() { // looks like a mallard } — RedheadDuck: display() { // looks like a redhead }
“All ducks quack and swim. The superclass takes care of the implementation code.”
“The display() method is abstract, since all duck subtypes look different.”
“Lots of other types of ducks inherit from the Duck class.” — “Each duck subtype is responsible for implementing its own display() behavior for how it looks on the screen.”
fly-feature: “What Joe added.” — Duck now has fly(), and “All subclasses inherit fly().”
“What we want.” — only ducks that actually fly should have it.
rubber-duck-flying: Joe: “Okay, so there’s a slight flaw in my design… I don’t… not all… should fly. When…?” (a rubber duck flapping through the air)
rubber-decoy-classes: RubberDuck: quack() { // squeak }, display() { // rubber duck }, fly() { // override to do nothing }
DecoyDuck: quack() { // override to do nothing }, display() { // decoy duck }, fly() { // override to do nothing }
“But then what happens when we add wooden decoy ducks to the program? They aren’t supposed to fly or quack…”
“I could always just override the fly() method in rubber duck, like I have with the quack() method…”
interface-design: Duck stays the superclass of all ducks; Flyable and Quackable are interfaces.
MallardDuck / RedheadDuck implement Flyable and Quackable; RubberDuck and DecoyDuck only implement Quackable.
Each duck still supplies its own display(); the interfaces carry fly() and quack() signatures.
mirror-change: “CHANGE (use a mirror to see the answer)” — the mirror spells out the chapter’s only constant.
pull-out-varies: “Pull out what varies” — the Duck class stays the superclass of all ducks, but we pull out the fly and quack behaviors and put them in another class structure.
“Various behavior implementations are going to live here.” — “Now flying and quacking each get their own set of classes.”
animal-example: Animal: makeSound() — Dog: makeSound() { bark(); } — Cat: makeSound() { meow(); }
bark() { // bark sound } and meow() { // meow sound } are the “concrete implementations”.
Neither animal overrides the other’s sound: each has its own implementation of the same method.
behaviors-diagram: <<interface>> FlyBehavior: fly() — implementations FlyWithWings and FlyNoWay
<<interface>> QuackBehavior: quack() — implementations Quack, Squeak and MuteQuack
“Here’s the implementation of flying for all ducks that have wings.” — “And here’s the implementation for all ducks that can’t fly.”
“Quacks that really quack.” — “Quacks that squeak.” — “Quacks that make no sound at all.”
duck-has-behavior: Duck now holds FlyBehavior flyBehavior and QuackBehavior quackBehavior; performFly() and performQuack() replace fly() and quack().
“Instance variables hold a reference to a specific behavior at runtime.”
“The behavior variables are declared as the behavior INTERFACE type.”
big-picture: Duck: swim(), display(), performQuack(), performFly(), setFlyBehavior(), setQuackBehavior(), // other duck-like methods…
<<interface>> FlyBehavior → FlyWithWings, FlyNoWay; <<interface>> QuackBehavior → Quack, Squeak, MuteQuack
MallardDuck, RedheadDuck, RubberDuck and DecoyDuck all extend Duck and implement display().
“Encapsulated fly behavior” and “Encapsulated quack behavior” — “Think of each set of behaviors as a family of algorithms.”
“These behavior ‘algorithms’ are interchangeable.” — “Client makes use of an encapsulated family of algorithms for both flying and quacking.”
Your job in the book’s exercise: write IS-A, HAS-A or IMPLEMENTS on every arrow.
guru: Guru: Tell me what you have learned of the Object-Oriented ways.
Student: Guru, I have learned that the promise of the object-oriented way is reuse.
Student: …through inheritance all good things may be reused and so we come to drastically cut development time like we swiftly cut bamboo in the woods.

Guru: Is more time spent on code before or after development is complete? — Student: The answer is after, Guru. We always spend more time maintaining and changing software than on initial development.
Guru: So, should effort go into reuse above maintainability and extensibility?
Guru: I can see that you still have much to learn. I would like for you to go and meditate on inheritance further.
ribbon-first: “You just applied your first design pattern—the STRATEGY Pattern. That’s right, you used the Strategy Pattern to rework the SimUDuck app.”
“Thanks to this pattern, the simulator is ready for any changes those execs might cook up on their next business trip to Maui.”
diner: Flo: “Give me a C.J. White, a black & white, a Jack Benny, a radio, a house boat, a coffee regular, and burn one!”

Alice: “I need a cream cheese with jelly on white bread, a chocolate soda with vanilla ice cream, a grilled cheese sandwich with bacon, a tuna fish salad on toast, a banana split with ice cream & sliced bananas, and a coffee with a cream and two sugars… oh, and put a hamburger on the grill!”
Same order, twice the words: Flo has a shared vocabulary with the short-order cook.
cubicle: Rick: “So I created this broadcast class. It keeps track of all the objects listening to it, and anytime a new piece of data comes along it sends a message to each listener. What’s cool is that the listeners can join the broadcast at any time or they can even remove themselves. It is really dynamic and loosely coupled!”
“Rick, why didn’t you just say you are using the Observer Pattern?”
“If you communicate in patterns, then other developers know immediately and precisely the design you’re describing.”
brain: “Your Code, now new and improved with design patterns!”
“Your BRAIN” vs “Your Code” — patterns go into your brain before they go into your code.
“Rework your old code when you find it’s degrading into an inflexible mess.”
toolbox: OO Basics: Abstraction, Encapsulation, Polymorphism, Inheritance
OO Principles: Encapsulate what varies. — Favor composition over inheritance. — Program to interfaces, not implementations.
OO Patterns: Strategy — defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable…
“We assume you know the OO basics like abstraction, encapsulation, polymorphism, and inheritance. If you are a little rusty… pull out your favorite object-oriented book and review.”
“Throughout the book, think about how patterns rely on OO basics and principles.”
crossword: “It’s your standard crossword; all of the solution words are from this chapter.” — the numbered squares are the crossword grid.
puzzle-pieces: KnifeBehavior (cutting with a knife), BowAndArrowBehavior (shooting an arrow with a bow), AxeBehavior (chopping with an axe), SwordBehavior (swinging a sword)
Character: WeaponBehavior weapon, setWeapon(WeaponBehavior w) { this.weapon = w; }, fight()
King, Queen, Knight and Troll each implement fight() { … }
puzzle-solution: Character HAS-A WeaponBehavior: fight() calls useWeapon() on the current weapon.
“Note that ANY object could implement the WeaponBehavior interface—say, a paper clip, a tube of toothpaste, or a mutated sea bass.”
